WORO DOWY Wilson has set the fashion in telling the truth about Washington. As a historian unswayed by emotion and kinded feelings, he has gone by the romance which has completely enveloped the character of our first President and drawn a picture of the man that has been altogether to be realistic for those worshipers who like halos with their heroes in history. As of the man, so of his movements has a deal of untruth been uttered. Rhode Island has contributed its share. All over the State, as all up and down the Atlantic coast, are houses in which it is valiantly asserted Washington once slept. Wherever one finds a house with the date of erection preceding the Revolution, one may confidently expect to hear that at such and such a time Washington was there and stayed through the night. But the facts do not make him out such a continuous and persistent sleeper. When the mists of tradition are brushed away, the record shows that there were just four places in the State, in which it is certain that Washington spent some time as a guest. Three were in Providence and one in East Greenwich. All claims of the rest to fame are of dubious foundation. Although Washington stayed several days on each of his visits to Newport, there is nothing to indicate where he rested 'o' might. That he spread his time as generously and as conveniently as he was able among several of the leading families there is little question. But neither he nor contemporary warries give any names; and to-day in Newport only. Trinity Church claims him as its own. Whether or not he went to church while in the town by the sea is a problem that may never be solved satisfactorily. The tradition of his visit to Trinity and of the pew he occupied has been paraded and then seemingly punctured so many times that any arbitrary attempt to settle it would revive a controversy that is better quiescent. It may be said in all fairness, however that the modern demand for historical fact regardless of romance has had its effect in the case of old Trinity and its cherished memory of the past. Washington liked Rhode Island and its hospitality. He had many friends here. Chief among them was Stephen Hopkins,
